summary: The patch relaxes the constraint-count guard from `!= 1` to `< 1`, which suppresses the crash but then unconditionally deletes only `constraint_names[0]` when multiple constraints match — and the introspection order is non-deterministic, so it may drop the unique_together's backing index instead of the intended index_together index. The correct, idiomatic fix is to make the lookup precise (pass `unique=False` in the `index` deletion path so exactly one constraint is found), keeping the strict guard intact.

issues.description: Wrong approach. When unique_together and index_together share columns, `_constraint_names(..., index=True)` returns 2 names (the _uniq backing index and the _idx). With `< 1`, the code falls through to `self.execute(self._delete_constraint_sql(sql, model, constraint_names[0]))` and deletes only the first. `_constraint_names` order is not deterministic, so this can delete the unique constraint's index rather than the index_together index. The accepted fix is to disambiguate the lookup (e.g. pass `{'index': True, 'unique': False}` to `_delete_composed_index` from `alter_index_together`) so exact

Behavioral regression / correctness risk: dropping the strict count check removes a useful safety net and can silently delete the wrong index. In the reported scenario the goal is to remove the index_together index while preserving the unique_together; deleting `constraint_names[0]` can instead remove the unique constraint's index, leaving the index_together in place and weakening the schema.

Incomplete: when more than one constraint matches, only one is ever deleted (the first), so the operation is neither a clean single-target delete nor a multi-delete. The fix should target precisely the index being removed rather than picking an arbitrary match.
